definitions.definition: The Goddess is the power of the absolute without which Śiva cannot stir (SL 1; Subhagodaya); she abides in all beings as consciousness (Devī Māhātmya 5).
She is citśakti and the form of sentience, yet also the power of the insentient (LSN 90); the self-awareness (vimarśa) of Śiva's light (KKV 2; LSN 112).

relations.note: Śakti is the vimarśa side of the one reality

definitions.definition: Lalitā is the qualityless, partless Brahman (LSN 43-45), consciousness and bliss seated on the five Brahmas (LSN 61), 'cit' being Brahman itself (Bhāskararāya on name 4), and at once the queen on Kāmeśvara's lap; the mahātattva meaning of the mantra is the partless supreme principle (YH 2.73-74).
The Śākta Upaniṣads have the Goddess declare herself Brahman (Devī, Bahvṛca Upaniṣads).

relations.note: the Śrīvidyā statement of the general Śākta doctrine

name: The union of Śiva and Śakti (śiva-śakti-aikya, sāmarasya)

definitions.definition: The Goddess's form is the oneness of Śiva and Śakti (LSN 183); Tripurā is the fusion of light and self-awareness (Dīpikā on YH 1.6); Śiva joined to Śakti can create, without her he cannot stir (SL 1).
Śiva and Śakti are equal in primacy, with fivefold equality (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 41).
Their union is the great point and the 'I' (KKV 4-5).

relations.note: the Samaya equality is set against the Kaula views

name: The fivefold equality of Śiva and Śakti (pañcavidha-sāmya)

definitions.definition: Samayā (the Goddess) and Samaya (Śiva) are equal in seat (adhiṣṭhāna), in state (avasthāna), in action (anuṣṭhāna), in form (rūpa) and in name (nāma), and so of equal primacy (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 41).
Bhāskararāya repeats the five equalities (seat of worship, acts such as creation, dance, names such as Bhairava, form such as redness), crediting the Subhagodaya commentator (on LSN 37).

Māyā is not an independent illusion but the Goddess's own power: she is Mahāmāyā, queen of the supreme Brahman, who makes the universe whirl (SL 98), 'of the form of both knowledge and ignorance' (LSN 87).
She herself becomes mind, space and the elements; nothing is beyond her transformation (SL 35); yet Bhāskararāya's tradition also names her 'substratum of the illusory world' (LSN 142).
The Kaula Upaniṣad: ignorance is knowledge, the world is the Lord, the impermanent is permanent — nothing is other than Śakti (with Bhāskararāya's gloss).

relations.note: Advaita's māyā is indeterminable and sublated by knowledge; the Śākta māyā is the real power of the Goddess

name: The Goddess's gentle and fierce forms

definitions.definition: One Goddess appears in gentle (saumya) forms — Lalitā, Umā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī — and fierce (ghora) forms — Durgā, Caṇḍikā, Kālī, Cāmuṇḍā; all goddesses and all women are her portions (Devī Māhātmya 11); knowers of the āgamas name her Speech, Padmā or Pārvatī, but she is 'a certain fourth' (SL 98).
Lalitā is the gentle, beautiful queen, but her war-names show fierce powers in her service — Vārāhī, Jvālāmālinī, the Nityās (LSN 25-33).

members: saumya: Lalitā, Umā, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Bālā
ghora/ugra: Durgā, Caṇḍikā, Kālī, Cāmuṇḍā, Vārāhī

definitions.definition: Creation, preservation, withdrawal, concealment and grace are done by the Goddess in the forms of Brahmā, Govinda, Rudra, Īśvara and Sadāśiva (LSN 63-64), each god acting on her command given by a flicker of her brows (SL 24).

relations.note: the same five acts, ascribed to the Goddess

definitions.definition: The Goddess's couch has Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra and Īśvara as its legs and Sadāśiva as its plank; without her they are corpses (LSN 61; PKS 3.10; SL 94).

The white and red points (Śiva and Śakti) and the point of their union, the sun that is the 'I'; kāma because it is lovely and kalā as the points of fire and moon; this vidyā is the sequence of the Goddess's cakra, and one who knows it becomes Mahātripurasundarī (KKV 6-8).
The Goddess 'whose form is the kāmakalā' (LSN 73); the Saundaryalaharī's meditation on it (SL 19) is taught for attraction.

name: The three cities (tripura) and their triads

definitions.definition: Tripurā is prior to every triad — abodes, principles, seats, liṅgas, letters (Dīpikā on YH 1.6); her city is threefold as triangle, circle and square and her mantra three-part (Bhāskararāya); she is 'trayī, abode of the three aims, dwelling in the three, garlanded by the three cities' (LSN 162-163) and 'trimūrti' (LSN 125); the Tripurā Upaniṣad opens with 'three cities, three paths'.
She existed before the three lights (Cidvallī on KKV 2).

notes: The association of the three cities with the three bodies and three states is a common traditional reading; the exact list varies by commentator.

definitions.definition: In the Prādhānika Rahasya the supreme Mahālakṣmī with the three qualities is the origin; from her arise Mahākālī and Mahāsarasvatī and from them the gods and their consorts.
Śailaputrī, Brahmacāriṇī, Candraghaṇṭā, Kūṣmāṇḍā, Skandamātā, Kātyāyanī, Kālarātri, Mahāgaurī and Siddhidātrī, named by Brahmā in the Devī Kavaca and worshipped one on each night of Navarātri.

name: The Goddess as Mahāmāyā and the supreme

definitions.definition: The Śākta hymns take up the Purāṇic Mahāmāyā: she makes the universe whirl as queen of the supreme Brahman (SL 98).
Śrīvidyā identifies Lalitā with Brahman beyond qualities and with the partless supreme principle (LSN 43-45; YH 2.73-74).
Tripurā is the fusion of prakāśa and vimarśa (Dīpikā on YH 1.6); Maheśa is pure light with self-awareness merged within, and Śakti the mirror of Śiva's form (KKV 1-3).
The 'I' (aham), union of the letters a and ha, the lump of Śiva and Śakti that has swallowed the worlds (KKV 5).

name: The states: waking, dream, deep sleep, the fourth and beyond

definitions.definition: The Goddess is Viśva in waking, Taijasa in dream, Prājña in sleep, the fourth, and devoid of all states (LSN 62-63); in inner worship the union of the three states is betel and the fourth is prostration (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).

name: The fourth and beyond the fourth (turīya, turīyātīta)

definitions.definition: The state beyond the fourth is reached by firmness in the fourth (Bhāskararāya on LSN 63).

name: The three powers: will, knowledge, action

definitions.definition: In the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad the power of action is the seat, kuṇḍalinī the power of knowledge is the house, and the power of will is Mahātripurasundarī herself.

name: Lalitā's four weapons as the mind's powers

definitions.definition: Her noose is attachment, her goad anger, her sugarcane bow the mind and her five flower-arrows the five subtle elements (LSN 2-3); in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad the bow is the mind, the arrows the five tanmātras, the noose attachment and the goad aversion.

name: The body as the Śrīcakra

definitions.definition: The guru is Śakti; the body with nine openings is the Śrīcakra; each enclosure and its deities are constituents of body and mind — the fourteen channels, ten vital airs, ten fires, the qualities, the subtle elements, the inner organ — and the fifteen Nityās are the lunar days (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).
The Samayin worships the cakra only within, in the heart and the crown (Lakṣmīdhara).

members: eight (cold, heat, pleasure, pain, desire, sattva, rajas, tamas) = Vaśinī etc.
unmanifest, mahat, ahaṃkāra = Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, Bhagamālinī

definitions.definition: The Goddess herself, dwelling in the mūlādhāra, piercing the knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra, mounting the thousand-petalled lotus, showering nectar and returning to sleep in the kula-pit in three and a half coils (LSN 38-40; SL 9-10); seen by the pure-minded as a digit slender as lightning above the six lotuses (SL 21).
The knots of Brahmā (after the mūlādhāra), Viṣṇu (after the maṇipūra) and Rudra (at the ājñā) pierced by the Goddess in her ascent (LSN 38-39).

Six centres below the thousand-petalled lotus; the Saundaryalaharī places earth in the mūlādhāra, water in the maṇipūra, fire in the svādhiṣṭhāna, air in the heart, space in the throat and mind between the brows (SL 9), and worships a Śiva-Śakti pair in each (SL 36-41).

Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara and Oḍḍiyāna, transformations of the four fused powers, located in the subtle body at kanda, pada, rūpa and beyond form (YH 1.41-42); the Goddess dwells in Jālandhara and Oḍyāṇa (LSN 82).

name: The ten mudrās of Śrīvidyā worship

definitions.definition: One seal for each enclosure plus a tenth: sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, sarvavidrāviṇī, sarvākarṣiṇī, sarvavaśaṅkarī, sarvonmādinī, sarvamahāṅkuśā, sarvakhecarī, sarvabījā, sarvayoni and sarvatrikhaṇḍā; the Goddess is 'worshipped with the ten mudrās', 'the yoni-mudrā', 'lady of the trikhaṇḍā' (LSN 179-180).
The universe is the thirty-six principles (PKS 1.4); the Śrīcakra is the cakra of the thirty-six principles (Dīpikā on YH 1.86).
Lakṣmīdhara holds that the twenty-five principles are accepted by all as Vedic, reads the thirty-six in their light, and places the Śiva-Śakti pair beyond as the twenty-sixth (on SL 11).
Śiva clothed in body and coverings is the jīva; without coverings he is Paraśiva (PKS 1.5).
The central point of the Śrīcakra (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 8) and the great point of the Kāmakalāvilāsa in which Śiva's light is reflected; the pair of white and red points (KKV 4-7).

Four upward Śiva triangles and five downward Śakti triangles interlock around the central point to make forty-three angles, surrounded by eight and sixteen petals, three circles and a square of three lines (SL 11); it arises as the supreme Śakti beholds her own vibrancy (YH 1.9-10) and is ninefold with nine mantras (YH 1.13); it is the Goddess's dwelling (LSN 182) and the body itself (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).
For the Samayins it is worshipped within and is the moon-disc in the crown (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 10).

name: The nine enclosures (āvaraṇa) of the Śrīcakra

definitions.definition: From outside in: (1) bhūpura, Trailokyamohana, cakreśvarī Tripurā, Prakaṭa yoginīs (the powers Aṇimā etc., the eight Mothers, the ten mudrā-powers); (2) sixteen petals, Sarvāśāparipūraka, Tripureśī, Gupta yoginīs (the sixteen attractions); (3) eight petals, Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa, Tripurasundarī, Guptatara (the eight Anaṅga goddesses); (4) fourteen triangles, Sarvasaubhāgyadāyaka, Tripuravāsinī, Sampradāya yoginīs; (5) outer ten, Sarvārthasādhaka, Tripurāśrī, Kulottīrṇa; (6) inner ten, Sarvarakṣākara, Tripuramālinī, Nigarbha; (7) eight triangles, Sarvarogahara, Tripurāsiddhā, Rahasya (the eight goddesses of speech); (8) the triangle, Sarvasiddhiprada, Tripurāmbā, Atirahasya (Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, Bhagamālinī); (9) the point, Sarvānandamaya, Mahātripurasundarī, Parāparātirahasya.

notes: Names of the cakras, cakreśvarīs and yoginī classes from memory of the standard navāvaraṇa-pūjā (PKS 5, Nityotsava); not checked verse by verse.

name: The three sections (kūṭa) of the Śrīvidyā mantra

definitions.definition: Vāgbhava (the Goddess's face), Kāmarāja or middle (neck to waist) and Śakti (below the waist); the mantra with its three sections is her subtle body (LSN 35-36); she is 'three-peaked' (LSN 118).

name: The fifteen- and sixteen-syllable Śrīvidyā (structure only)

definitions.definition: The Pañcadaśī has fifteen syllables in three sections, each closed by the seed called hṛllekhā (SL 32); a further seed added makes the sixteen-syllable Ṣoḍaśī (LSN 118); in the Kādi form the first section begins with 'ka', in the Hādi form with 'ha'; the Triśatī unfolds the fifteen syllables in three hundred names. Syllables are deliberately not recorded here.

The two living forms of the vidyā: Kādi, after Manmatha (Kāmarāja), taught by the Tantrarāja ('Kādimata') and encoded in SL 32; Hādi, after Lopāmudrā. The Bhāvanā Upaniṣad teaches its contemplation 'according to the Kādi and Hādi doctrines'; the twelve upāsakas each have their own form.

name: The twelve great worshippers of Śrīvidyā

definitions.definition: Manu, Candra, Kubera, Lopāmudrā, Manmatha, Agastya, Agni, Sūrya, Indra, Skanda, Śiva and Krodhabhaṭṭāraka (Durvāsas), each with a form of the vidyā, derived in the Jñānārṇava (Bhāskararāya).

name: The six meanings of the mantra (Yoginīhṛdaya)

definitions.definition: Literal (bhāvārtha), traditional (sampradāyārtha), hidden (nigarbha: Śiva, guru and self), Kaula (the unity of cakra, deity, vidyā, guru and self), all-secret, and great-principle meaning (the partless supreme) (YH 2.15-16, 2.48, 2.51-52, 2.73-74).

name: The fifteen meanings of the Pañcadaśī (Varivasyārahasya)

definitions.definition: The Gāyatrī meaning, the six Yoginīhṛdaya meanings, and the meanings of the name, of the sound-form, of part of the name, of the Śaktas, of fusion, the collective, the qualified and the great-saying meaning (VR 57-59); knowing them is required, since recitation without meaning bears no fruit (VR 54-56).

relations.note: the six YH meanings are included among the fifteen

name: The subtle phases of pronouncing the mantra (bindu to unmanā)

definitions.definition: Bindu, ardhacandra, rodhinī, nāda, nādānta, śakti, vyāpikā, samanā and unmanā, each half the length of the one before, unmanā being timeless (Varivasyārahasya with Prakāśa).

name: The letters as the fifty seats

definitions.definition: The Goddess is 'of the form of the fifty seats' (LSN 156): the fifty letters of the alphabet as sacred seats; the mātṛkā is placed on the disciple at initiation (PKS 1.38-39).

Vaśinī, Kāmeśvarī, Modinī, Vimalā, Aruṇā, Jayinī, Sarveśvarī, Kaulinī: composers of the Sahasranāma, deities of the eight-triangle enclosure, givers of poetry (SL 17), and in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad cold, heat, pleasure, pain, desire and the three qualities.

name: Maṇidvīpa and Śrīnagara, the Goddess's world

definitions.definition: The jewel island in the ocean of nectar with its wish-tree gardens and palace of wish-gems (SL 8; Devī Bhāgavata 12.10-12).

Śrīnagara on Meru's central peak with its enclosures, the Cintāmaṇi palace whose four doors are the four āmnāyas, and the couch of five corpses, visualized in worship with forty-four mantras (LSN 21-23; PKS 3.10).

name: The fifteen Nityās

definitions.definition: Kāmeśvarī, Bhagamālinī, Nityaklinnā, Bheruṇḍā, Vahnivāsinī, Mahāvajreśvarī, Śivadūtī, Tvaritā, Kulasundarī, Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, Sarvamaṅgalā, Jvālāmālinī and Citrā, around Tripurasundarī the sixteenth; the Vāmakeśvara and Tantrarāja give their mantras and rites; the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad makes them the fifteen lunar days.

notes: Order and some names from memory (PKS 4 lists them with mantras, not reproduced).

name: The Nityās as the lunar days and time

definitions.definition: The fifteen Nityās are the fifteen lunar days, the unfolding of time (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad); the Śrīvidyā's digits wax and wane with the moon over sixteen days, so the moon is the Śrīcakra (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 10); the Tantrarāja correlates the Nityās with days and breaths.

The cakra — the universe of thirty-six principles — arises when the supreme Śakti beholds her own vibrancy (YH 1.9-10); the Goddess transforms herself into mind and the elements (SL 35); she arose from the fire-altar of consciousness (LSN 1).
Paraśiva's light reflected in the mirror of vimarśa becomes the great point, whence the 'I' and the world of word and meaning (KKV 4-7).
The Goddess alone existed in the beginning and produced the egg and the gods (Bahvṛca Upaniṣad).
The Sahasranāma recounts the war in names: Mantriṇī and Daṇḍanāthā, the fire-wall, Gaṇeśa from Kāmeśvara's glance, the destruction of Bhaṇḍa and the revival of Kāma (LSN 25-33).

Promised by knowledge of the cakra-code (YH 1.86) and of the worship-code (YH 3.1), by three muhūrtas of the Bhāvanā contemplation, and to the steadfast practitioner wherever he dies (PKS 10.82); it is release from the eight bonds (Dīpikā); the Rudrayāmala places it at the end of the ladder of births (Bhāskararāya).

name: Five kinds of liberation (sārṣṭi, sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya, sāyujya)

definitions.definition: The knower of the Śiva-Śakti pair beyond the principles attains, according to the degree of worship, the five liberations: equal power, same world, nearness, same form and union (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 11); union is granted even to one who says 'Bhavāni tvam' (SL 22).

relations.note: adds sārṣṭi (equality of power) to the usual four

name: Enjoyment and liberation as the twofold goal (bhukti-mukti)

definitions.definition: The Goddess's tantra alone accomplishes all the aims of life (SL 31); her worshipper enjoys Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī and, freed of bonds, tastes the supreme Brahman (SL 99); saubhāgya names this double blessing.

name: Death and dissolution in Śākta teaching

definitions.definition: For the steadfast knower the place of death makes no difference — an outcaste's house or Kāśī — for he is liberated while living (PKS 10.82); the Kaula Upaniṣad teaches liberation in this very body without departure on the path of the gods (with Bhāskararāya); at the great dissolution all the gods perish while the Goddess's consort sports on (SL 26).

name: The three codes (saṅketa): cakra, mantra, worship

definitions.definition: The teaching of Tripurā is a threefold code — of the cakra, the mantra and worship (YH 1.6) — a 'tryst' where Śiva and Śakti meet (Dīpikā); knowing the cakra-code and worship-code makes one liberated while living.

name: The three kinds of worship (parā, parāparā, aparā)

definitions.definition: Parā: abiding in non-duality across all the senses' outflows; parāparā: meditative dissolution of outer into the inner non-dual abode; aparā: worship of the cakra, done even by Śiva and by all knowers because it yields the conviction of non-difference (YH 3.2-3 with the Dīpikā).

name: The unity of guru, mantra, deity and self

definitions.definition: Knowledge of the inner self comes from realizing the oneness of guru, mantra, deity, self, mind and breath (PKS 1.11); the Kaula meaning of the mantra is the unity of cakra, deity, vidyā, guru and self (YH 2.51-52).

name: Samaya and Kaula modes of worship

definitions.definition: Samaya worship is in the inner space of the heart and crown; Kaula worship uses an external support; the Samayin rejects outer worship, the Kaula rites and the sixty-four tantras (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 8, 31, 41).
The Goddess is both Kaulinī and intent on Samaya conduct, worshipped on the right and left paths (LSN 36-37, 169-171); Bhāskararāya defines the two modes without rejecting either.
Outer cakra worship is performed by Śiva himself and by all knowers (YH 3.3 with the Dīpikā).

Two Kaula doctrines set out by Lakṣmīdhara before the Samaya view: the pūrva-Kaula on the Goddess as Śiva's body with a shared relation of principal and subsidiary (SL 34), and the uttara-Kaula in which there is no Śiva-principle apart from Śakti and she alone is worshipped (SL 23, 35).

Bliss is the form of Brahman residing in the body; the five 'M's (wine, meat, fish, grain or gesture, union) manifest it and are used in secret, exposure leading to hell (PKS 1.12); the daily worship continues without them when they are unavailable (PKS 1.24); the Tripurā Upaniṣad (12) speaks of such offerings. Summary only.
Rejected by the Samaya school as non-Vedic (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 41).

name: The conduct of the Śrīvidyā initiate

definitions.definition: No censure of other schools or persons, secrecy toward the unqualified, constant immersion in Śiva-hood, avoidance of the six passions, unsanctioned violence and theft, worship of one guru without doubt, non-possessiveness, action without regard to fruit, fearlessness (PKS 1.14-25); inwardly Śākta, outwardly Śaiva, among people Vaiṣṇava (Kaula Upaniṣad).

name: All schools valid for their qualified followers

definitions.definition: Bhāskararāya: the many schools are valid for their respective qualified followers; censuring them unsettles those followers, who then fall from both their own school and the Kaula, for which they are not qualified (on the Kaula Upaniṣad); hence Paraśurāma's rule of no censure (PKS 1.14).

The Yoginīhṛdaya is to be guarded with special care (YH 1.2); the Veda is public like a courtesan while this vidyā is hidden in all the schools (PKS 1.30); secrets are told only to a worthy disciple (PKS 1.16; Kaula Upaniṣad); exposure of the Kaula worship leads to hell (PKS 1.12); 'secret' finally means the identity of self and supreme (Bhāskararāya).

Śāktī by the entry of power, śāmbhavī by the placing of the guru's foot, māntrī by imparting mantra (PKS 1.32); the guru burns the disciple's bonds with a wave of light, gives Bālā and a name ending in '-ānandanātha' and makes the disciple his own self (PKS 1.35-43).

name: The three streams of gurus (divya, siddha, mānava)

definitions.definition: The guru-lineage worshipped in Śrīvidyā is divided into the divine stream (divyaugha), the perfected stream (siddhaugha) and the human stream (mānavaugha); the Goddess is 'of the form of the circle of gurus' (LSN 138); the mind's flow toward the meaning comes only by the guru's grace (Setubandha).

The guru is the Śakti that is the cause of all (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad); one guru is worshipped without doubt (PKS 1.20); the teaching is given only to a worthy disciple (PKS 1.16); at initiation the guru makes the disciple his own self (PKS 1.42); those without lineage who are proud of book-knowledge are harmed (YH 2.81).
Paramaśiva set forth five transmissions through his five faces (PKS 1.2); the four doors of the Goddess's palace are the eastern, southern, western and northern transmissions (PKS 3.10).
The two great families of Śākta tantra: the Śrīkula centred on Tripurasundarī (Śrīvidyā) and the Kālīkula centred on Kālī and related goddesses.

name: The Śākta Upaniṣads

definitions.definition: The Upaniṣads of the Muktikā canon devoted to the Goddess — Sītā, Annapūrṇā, Tripurātāpinī, Devī, Tripurā, Bhāvanā, Saubhāgyalakṣmī, Sarasvatīrahasya, Bahvṛca — read by Śrīvidyā as its śruti; Bhāskararāya commented on the Tripurā, Bhāvanā and Kaula Upaniṣads.

notes: Membership from memory of the Muktikā grouping; U04 owns the texts.

definitions.definition: The saṃhitās of Vasiṣṭha, Sanaka, Śuka, Sanandana and Sanatkumāra, teaching the Vedic Samaya way that Lakṣmīdhara follows (on SL 31); Bhāskararāya also calls them 'Samaya' (on LSN 37).

name: The sixty-four tantras of the Śākta lists

definitions.definition: The Saundaryalaharī says Paśupati beguiled the world with sixty-four tantras aimed at particular powers, then at the Goddess's insistence brought down her tantra, which alone accomplishes all aims (SL 31).
Kula is Śakti and akula Śiva, their relation kaula; the Goddess is Kaulinī and also akulā (Bhāskararāya on LSN 36-37).
See cpt:srividya-secrecy: the vidyā hidden in all schools (PKS 1.30) and guarded (YH 1.2).

name: Powers (siddhi) in Śrīvidyā and their place

definitions.definition: The eight powers Aṇimā and the rest are deities of the outermost enclosure, the gate where the gods won their powers (SL 93) and rays of the Goddess's own body (SL 96); firm contemplation brings the power of command (PKS 1.13); meditation with the goddesses of speech brings poetry (SL 17) and on the kāmakalā the power to attract (SL 19); the sixty-four tantras aim at particular powers, while the Goddess's tantra accomplishes all aims (SL 31); those who grasp the mantra without lineage are harmed by its rays (YH 2.81).
